content:
Let \(v(n)\) be the parity vector of the exponents of primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) in \(n\).  
A product of three distinct selected numbers is a square iff their parity vectors sum to \(0\).

A valid subset of size \(10\) is
\[
S=\{1,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14\}.
\]
Its parity vectors are
\[
0,0,\ e_3,\ e_5,\ e_2+e_3,\ e_7,\ e_2+e_5,\ e_{11},\ e_{13},\ e_2+e_7.
\]
The only forbidden nonzero triples among available types are
\[
\{e_2,e_3,e_2+e_3\},\ \{e_2,e_5,e_2+e_5\},\ \{e_2,e_7,e_2+e_7\},\ \{e_3,e_5,e_3+e_5\},\ \{e_2+e_3,e_2+e_5,e_3+e_5\}.
\]
None is fully present, and only two square vectors \(0\) are chosen, so no triple has product a square.

For an upper bound: at most two zero-vector numbers can be chosen. If a zero-vector number is chosen, at most one from each of \(\{2,8\}\) and \(\{3,12\}\) can be chosen. Excluding the isolated types \(11,13\), among the remaining eight constrained types at most six can be chosen without completing one of the five forbidden triples above. Thus the total is at most
\[
2+2+6=10.
\]
So the largest possible size is \(10\), achieved by the subset above.

\[
\boxed{\{1,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,13,14\}}
\]
